[THOUGHT] The history — chronic (2 years) itchy, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on elbows, knees and buttocks — is highly characteristic of plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris). Lack of reported nail or joint symptoms does not exclude psoriasis. Other diagnoses (eczema, tinea) are less likely given the distribution, chronicity, and classic scale. I have enough information to reach a conclusive most-likely diagnosis.

[FINISH]

[THOUGHT] The patient has a two‑year history of pruritic, well‑demarcated erythematous plaques with silver scaling located on classic extensor sites (elbows, knees) and buttocks. The chronicity, distribution, and description of silver/white scale are most characteristic of chronic plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris). Lack of reported nail or joint symptoms does not exclude psoriasis — nail involvement and psoriatic arthritis are common but not required for the diagnosis. Other possibilities (atopic dermatitis, tinea corporis, lichen planus, seborrheic dermatitis) are less likely given the extensor/buttock distribution and the classic silver scaling. Confirmation would be clinical on exam (Auspitz/Koebner signs), and biopsy or KOH testing only if atypical or diagnostic uncertainty.

[DIAGNOSIS] Chronic plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris)

[THOUGHT] The history (chronic, pruritic, well-located red plaques with silver scales on elbows, knees, buttocks for ~2 years) is highly suggestive of chronic plaque psoriasis. However, there are no objective examination findings, no photos, no KOH/fungal testing to exclude tinea, and no documentation of classic supportive signs (well-demarcated plaques, silvery scale, Auspitz sign, Koebner phenomenon, nail pitting, scalp/intergluteal involvement). No prior treatment response or family history is recorded. No joint exam or inflammatory markers were done to exclude psoriatic arthritis. Because the clinician did not document a skin exam or perform basic confirmatory/ exclusion tests, the data are insufficient for a conclusive diagnosis.

Red-flag or critical missing items: formal dermatologic exam (lesion morphology, distribution, BSA), nail and scalp assessment, KOH/prep or fungal culture if atypical, skin biopsy if uncertain, joint exam and brief PsA screen, documentation of prior treatments and responses, and photographs.

- Focused skin examination: precise lesion description (well-demarcated erythematous plaques, scale character), distribution, body surface area, and photographs.
- Nail exam (pitting, onycholysis), scalp and intergluteal/perianal assessment.
- Ask about family history of psoriasis and any prior treatments and responses.
- Quick psoriatic arthritis screen: targeted joint history and physical exam; consider CRP/ESR and rheumatology referral if positive.
- If lesions are atypical or diagnosis unclear, perform KOH scraping to exclude tinea and/or a skin biopsy for histopathology.
Provide these data and then reassess — with typical exam findings a clinical diagnosis of chronic plaque psoriasis would be acceptable; otherwise further testing may be required.
